commentary.text: Red advances directly into the center, claiming the first key square while preserving clear lanes for Yellow to support the center-occupation threat.

**Move note.** Red opened by driving a piece from (0,3) straight to (3,3), planting a flag on one of the four central squares. That matters more than it looks: if Team A ever holds all of (3,3), (3,4), (4,3), (4,4) at once, they win instantly, no captures required. So the center is not a "nice to have" — it is a live win condition I have to contest immediately.

I'm taking (4,4) with the Blue piece from (4,7). The row is clear, so the move is legal, and it does three things. It denies Team A the four-square set as long as I hold it. It sits diagonally opposite Red's piece, which means Red cannot sandwich it with the piece it already committed — sandwiches are strictly orthogonal, and there is no Red piece on either side of (4,4) along a row or column. And it opens the door for Green to drop into (4,3) next turn, giving my team two of the four central squares.

I checked the immediate danger before committing. To capture (4,4) by sandwich, Red needs same-colored pieces at both (3,4) and (5,4), or both (4,3) and (4,5); Red has none of those and cannot create two in one move. Enclosure would require every neighbor of (4,4) occupied, which is four moves away. The one line I'm watching is the row-4 axis: if I add Green at (4,3), an opponent piece landing on (4,5) with a matching piece on (4,2) would sweep both of my pieces at once, since sandwich lines happily mix my two colors. Red can reach (4,5) down column 5 and (4,2) down column 2, so that's a two-move plan I'll have a turn to break — simplest answer is to vacate (4,4) upward, which snaps the line, or to occupy one of those squares first.

Longer-term shape for this game: hold at least one center square at all times to veto their instant win, keep my two colors from lining up in capturable pairs, and look for the moment Red's advanced piece is stranded far from support so I can flank it with two Blues.
Yellow joins Red in the center at (4,3). This secures a second central square and also sets a potential Yellow sandwich across Blue’s piece on (4,4).

**Move note.** Yellow answered by dropping a piece onto (4,3), so Team A now holds two of the four central squares — (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow — while I hold (4,4). Two things are now urgent: my Blue on (4,4) is one Yellow move from dying (Yellow slides (7,5) up to (4,5) and the Blue piece is pinched between two Yellows along row 4), and I need a real counter-threat rather than pure defence.

The counter-threat is the point of this move. Red's (3,3) and Yellow's (4,3) are stacked vertically in column 3, and a sandwich line is allowed to contain *mixed* enemy colors — it only cares that every piece in the line is not my moving color and that the far end is. So if I own both (2,3) and (5,3) with Green, the line (3,3)-(4,3) is flanked by Green at both ends and **both** pieces come off the board in a single move: one loss for Red, one for Yellow, and both of their central squares vacated at once. Green from (2,0) travels a clear row 2 to take the first anchor.

I chose the top anchor rather than the bottom one deliberately. The follow-up runs Green (5,0) along row 5 to (5,3), and the only way to stop that is to plug (5,1) or (5,2) — squares that only Yellow can reach quickly, and Yellow doesn't move until after Red. Had I taken (5,3) first, Red moves next and could plug row 2 immediately with a single drop down column 2.

Safety check on (2,3): to pinch it, Red needs pieces on both (1,3) and (3,3). It has (3,3), but nothing can reach (1,3) in one move — no Red sits on row 1, and the only Red in column 3 is the one at (3,3), which is walled off by the piece I'm placing. The alternative pinch, (2,2) plus (2,4), takes Red two moves.

As for the threatened Blue on (4,4): I intend to answer that next turn by planting a Blue on (5,5), which shuts the column-5 highway Yellow needs to reach (4,5). That keeps my Green free for the capture. If instead they defuse by pulling either central piece away, they hand me the square and I walk into the middle.
Red develops to (2,2), placing a same-color flank beside Green’s advanced piece. This creates a coming sandwich threat on (2,3) while keeping Red’s central piece in place.

**Move note.** Two threats are now on the board and I have to weigh them. Red dropped a piece to (2,2), which sets up a row-2 pinch on my Green at (2,3): if Red also reaches (2,4) — one clear slide down column 4 — my Green is flanked and dies. Separately, my Blue on (4,4) is still one Yellow move from death, because Yellow sits on (4,3) and can run (7,5) straight up column 5 to (4,5), pinching my Blue between two Yellows.

The Yellow threat fires next; the Red threat needs one more turn. So I answer the faster one, and I answer it by shutting the road rather than by retreating. Blue steps from (5,7) to (5,5), which plugs column 5 at row 5 and leaves Yellow with no one-move path to (4,5). Row 4 from the right is empty of Yellows, and column 5 from above only reaches Red — and a Red on (4,5) is harmless, since a sandwich needs *both* flanks to match the mover's color, and (4,3) is Yellow. Mixed enemy colors do not pair up. That is the same asymmetry I intend to exploit all game.

Crucially, this keeps my Green free. The column-3 double capture is still armed: Green from (5,0) has a clear row 5 to (5,3), and landing there flanks the Red on (3,3) and the Yellow on (4,3) against my Green already sitting on (2,3) — both come off in one stroke, one loss charged to each enemy color, and both of their central squares emptied. Note the timing: Red's pinch on my (2,3) Green can only land after my next Green turn, so even in the worst case I collect two pieces before paying one.

I deliberately rejected blocking (2,4) with my own piece. It looks like it saves the Green, but it makes things far worse — with Red on (2,2), a Red arriving at (2,5) would sweep a line of Blue-then-Green back to its own piece, since a sandwich line happily mixes my two colors, and Red reaches (2,5) in a single move down column 5. Two pieces for one tempo is not a trade I'll offer.

If Yellow ignores everything and defuses by pulling (4,3) away, it surrenders a central square and I occupy it with Green from (4,0), where it will sit safely flanked by mismatched enemy colors.

Yellow steps to (5,3), breaking Green’s threatened vertical sandwich through the two central team pieces. It also blocks Green’s easiest landing square and keeps Yellow active near Blue’s advanced piece.

**Move note.** Yellow pulled back from (4,3) to (5,3) to dodge the column-3 double sandwich — but retreating out of the line left the Red piece on (3,3) hanging, because my Green on (2,3) is still sitting above it.

Green slides from (4,0) along the empty row 4 into (4,3). Looking up from the landing square: (3,3) is Red — not my color, so it starts a line — and immediately beyond it, (2,3) is my own Green. Line flanked at both ends by Green, so the Red piece is captured and removed. That is Red's first loss; two more and Red is eliminated outright.

The positional payoff is bigger than the piece. Red is now off the center entirely, and Team B holds two of the four winning squares — Green on (4,3) and Blue on (4,4), sitting side by side and mutually protecting each other. Note how solid that pair is: to pinch my Green along row 4 an enemy needs (4,2) *and* (4,4), but (4,4) is mine; to pinch it vertically it needs (3,3) *and* (5,3), and while Yellow holds (5,3), Yellow physically cannot reach (3,3) — column 3 is blocked by the Green I just placed, and no Yellow stands on row 3. The same logic shields my Blue on (4,4) from every direction.

That leaves (3,3) and (3,4) as the last two squares of an instant win. Blue has a clear run from (3,7) to (3,4), and Green on (3,0) now has a completely open row 3 to (3,3) since the Red blocker is gone. Two moves from victory, with two enemy turns to stop me — they will have to spend both on blocking, and anything they drop onto (3,4) I can take immediately by dropping a Blue on (2,4), pinching it against my Blue at (4,4).

I'm aware Red can still pinch my Green on (2,3) by reaching (2,4). I'm accepting that: I collect a Red piece and a central square now, and the piece they win back costs them the tempo I need in the middle.

Red completes the prepared sandwich on row 2: landing at (2,4) uses Red at (2,2) as the far flank and removes Green’s advanced piece at (2,3), dismantling the formation that just captured the central Red.

**Move note.** The center is now three-quarters mine to take. Green holds (4,3), Blue holds (4,4), and both (3,3) and (3,4) sit empty. Red spent its turn winning back my Green on (2,3), which was the price I accepted — but it means Red is not on the center at all, and the turn order now runs Blue, Yellow, Green. Only *one* enemy move stands between me and the fourth square.

Blue runs from (3,7) down the empty row 3 to (3,4). That is three of the four winning squares, and next turn Green from (3,0) has a completely clear row 3 straight into (3,3) — which ends the game immediately.

I took (3,4) rather than (3,3) on purpose. My Green on (3,0) approaches from the left, so if Blue occupied (3,3) it would wall my own Green out of (3,4) and the plan collapses. Taking the far square keeps the near one reachable.

Yellow's problem is that it has almost no legal answer. It cannot occupy (3,3): the only Yellow anywhere near column 3 is on (5,3), and my Green on (4,3) blocks it from coming up, while no Yellow stands on row 3. It cannot capture anything I hold either — pinching my Green on (4,3) needs both (3,3) and (5,3), and it can't reach (3,3); pinching either Blue needs squares that are already occupied by my own pieces, and both flanks of a sandwich must match the *mover's* color, so Red's piece on (2,4) is no help to Yellow at all. My three central pieces interlock and defend one another by simply existing.

That leaves exactly one defence: throw a piece up column 1 or column 2 to stand on (3,1) or (3,2) and block my Green's road. I expect that, and it costs Yellow a piece stranded deep on my side of the board with no support. If it comes, I'll switch to the slower route — Blue to row 1, then down column 3 into (3,3) — and keep the same square under attack from a second direction.
Yellow moves to (3,2) to block Green’s open row-3 route into (3,3), preventing Team B from completing all four central squares next turn. Yellow is also positioned to contest (3,3) directly.

**Move note.** Yellow's block on (3,2) did more than shut my Green out of row 3 — it created a genuine threat I have to respect. From (3,2), Yellow can step one square right to (3,3), and from there look down: my Green on (4,3) sits directly below, with a Yellow already waiting on (5,3). That's a clean sandwich — it would take my Green, put Yellow on the last central square, and unravel my whole center hold in a single move.

So I break the sandwich at its far end instead of retreating. Green runs from (6,0) along the empty row 6 to (6,3). Landing there, I look up: (5,3) is Yellow, and immediately beyond it is my own Green on (4,3) — the Yellow is flanked and captured. Yellow takes its first loss, and more importantly the anchor that made (3,3) dangerous is gone. If Yellow still steps into (3,3) now, it captures nothing: below it would be my Green on (4,3) with an empty square behind, and to its right my Blue on (3,4) with an empty square behind that.

My center trio — Green (4,3), Blue (4,4), Blue (3,4) — remains intact and still interlocks. Each one's flanking squares are occupied by another of my own pieces, and since a sandwich needs both ends to match the *mover's* color, Red's pieces on (2,2) and (2,4) can never combine with a Yellow to hurt me.

(3,3) is still the square that ends the game, and I now have two ways to keep pressing it. If Yellow parks there, I can take it: Green from (1,0) can run to (1,3) and drop to (2,3), pinching a Yellow on (3,3) against my Green on (4,3); or Blue can swing via row 6 to column 2 and come up to (3,2), pinching it against my Blue on (3,4). If Yellow doesn't park there, I need only get one piece down column 3 and the game is over.

Score after this: Red down one, Yellow down one, and I'm down one Green — with a far better position.

Red develops to (4,5), forming one end of a pincer across Green and Blue on the central row. If Yellow clears (3,2), Red can bring the piece on (2,2) to (4,2) and sandwich both central blockers together, forcing the opponents to break their center formation.

**Move note.** Red's jump to (4,5) was the real story of that turn, and it was aimed at my center block. With a Red anchored on (4,5), any Red piece that reaches (4,2) would look right along row 4 and see Green-(4,3), Blue-(4,4), then its own piece — a single move sweeping **two** of my pieces off the board. Red can't get to (4,2) yet (column 2 is plugged by Yellow's own piece on (3,2), and row 4 is walled by my pieces), but the route opens the moment Yellow steps aside, or in two moves via (0,1) down column 1 to (4,1) and then sideways.

Rather than defend that square, I remove the anchor. Blue steps from (3,4) to (3,5) and looks down: (4,5) is Red, and directly beyond it sits my Blue on (5,5). The Red piece is flanked and captured. Red is now on **two** losses — one more and Red is eliminated, at which point every remaining Red piece turns Void and can never capture again. That would strip Team A of most of its teeth.

Yes, this gives up (3,4). I judged that cheap. I was holding three central squares but had no way to reach the fourth — (3,3) is screened by Yellow on (3,2) from the left and by my own Green on (4,3) from below — so the center hold was a blockade, not a winning threat, and Team A occupies none of the four squares, so there's no race to lose. Material and the elimination clock are the live currencies now.

The square is also poisoned for Red. If Red drops from (2,4) into (3,4), I answer with Blue (2,7) to (2,4), pinching it against my Blue on (4,4) — that's Red's third loss and the elimination. Any Red arriving there from another direction runs into the same pincer, or into (3,3)-versus-(3,5) with my new Blue as the far flank.

And the row-4 disaster is now dead: with (4,5) empty, a Red on (4,2) sees Green, Blue, then an empty square, and captures nothing.
Yellow takes (3,3), using the central vacancy Blue created while capturing Red. This blocks Team B’s center plan and establishes a secure foothold from which Yellow can pressure Blue on row 3.

**Move note.** Yellow slid from (3,2) into (3,3), grabbing the one central square I couldn't reach. That's the square the whole game turns on: I hold (4,3) and (4,4), and (3,4) is empty and reachable, so if I can clear (3,3) and fill both, the game ends instantly.

The good news is that Yellow parked itself directly above my Green on (4,3), which makes it capturable by the very piece it's leaning on. A sandwich needs both flanking pieces to match the mover's color, and I already own the bottom flank in Green. So a Green landing on (2,3) looks down, sees Yellow on (3,3), and immediately beyond it my own Green on (4,3) — Yellow captured, square cleared. Note the line stops at my own piece rather than running through it, so there's no friendly-fire risk to (4,3).

Green from (1,0) runs the empty row 1 to (1,3) to get into position for exactly that drop. From there it is one step down column 3 to the capture. If it lands, Yellow goes to two losses and (3,3) opens up — and I'd then have two easy fills, Green from (2,3) stepping down into (3,3) and Blue from (3,5) sliding into (3,4), which is the win.

(1,3) is safe for now: pinching it needs matching pieces on both (1,2) and (1,4), or both (0,3) and (2,3), and neither Red nor Yellow owns a single one of those squares yet.

The other clock I'm running is Red's. Red is on two losses — one more and it's eliminated, turning every Red piece Void and permanently unable to capture. Red's piece on (2,4) is the target: Blue to (1,4) and then Blue from (3,5) into (3,4) pinches it vertically, and that second move also retakes a central square. So my Blue and Green plans point at the same region and reinforce each other.

If Red blocks (2,3), it costs Red a tempo and usually shifts a piece off the target square I want elsewhere; if Yellow retreats to (2,3) instead, it abandons (3,3) and I can take it with my Green from (4,3), capturing on arrival, then refill from (6,3).
Red moves into (3,4), joining Yellow in the center and placing Blue on (3,5) under a direct sandwich threat: the remaining edge Red can later land on (3,6) with this Red as the far flank.

**Move note.** Red walked into it. Dropping from (2,4) to (3,4) put a Red piece directly above my Blue on (4,4), and (2,4) — the square on the far side — was left completely empty with a clear road along row 2 from my Blue on (2,7).

So Blue runs (2,7) to (2,4) and looks down: (3,4) is Red, and immediately beyond it sits my own Blue on (4,4). Both flanks are mine, so the Red piece is captured. That is **Red's third loss — Red is eliminated.**

This is the biggest swing of the game so far. Every Red piece still on the board turns Void: they keep taking turns and can still shuffle around to block squares, but a Void piece triggers no capture check at all when it moves. It can never take one of my pieces again. Team A's entire offense is now a single color — Yellow — which already carries one loss. Two more Yellow captures and both enemy colors are eliminated, which wins outright.

It also reopens the center. The four squares now read: Yellow on (3,3), empty (3,4), my Green on (4,3), my Blue on (4,4). Blue on (3,5) is one step from retaking (3,4), and Yellow's piece on (3,3) is still leaning on my Green — a Green landing on (2,3) pinches it against my Green on (4,3) and clears the last square. My Green already sits on (1,3), one step above that landing spot.

So I have two convergent routes. If Yellow retreats from (3,3) up to (2,3) to deny me the drop, it abandons the central square and I take it with Green from (4,3), capturing the Yellow on arrival against my Green on (1,3) — and my spare Green on (6,3) refills (4,3) up the empty column. Either branch costs Yellow a piece and hands me a central square.

I checked Yellow's replies before committing: nothing of mine can be pinched next turn, since every sandwich Yellow wants needs two matching Yellows and it can only place one per turn, and Red's Void pieces cannot help it.

Yellow shifts to (3,4), staying in the center while closing the gap beside Blue on (3,5). This prepares a Yellow landing on (3,6) that would sandwich that Blue piece, forcing it to respond or concede a loss.

**Move note.** Yellow shifted from (3,3) to (3,4), and that single step created two immediate capture threats against me, both using that same Yellow piece as the far anchor. Running (7,4) up column 4 to (5,4) would pinch my Blue on (4,4) against it; running (7,6) up column 6 to (3,6) would pinch my Blue on (3,5) against it. I can only shut one road with this move.

I'm saving (4,4). It's one of the four winning squares, and — more importantly — it's half of the mechanism I intend to win with. Green slides from (5,0) across the empty row 5 to (5,4), plugging column 4 so nothing can come up from row 7. The square is completely immune: pinching it vertically needs (4,4), which is my own Blue, and horizontally needs (5,5), also my own Blue.

Here's the machine I'm building. Yellow's piece on (3,4) now sits with my Blue on (2,4) above it and my Blue on (4,4) below it. Captures only fire on the moving side's landing square, so it's safe sitting there — but only until I *re-enter*. If I step the (2,4) Blue up to (1,4) and then drop it back onto (2,4), that landing looks down and sees Yellow-then-my-own-Blue: captured. Two Blue moves, entirely under my control, and Yellow can't refill (3,4) from below because my own pieces wall column 4, or from above because it has nothing there.

And that piece is effectively frozen. Once my Green comes down column 3 to (3,3), I'll hold three of the four central squares, so the moment Yellow's piece leaves (3,4) I simply drop a Blue in from (2,4) and the game ends. It must stand still and be taken.

Yellow is on one loss. The capture takes it to two, and with Red already eliminated, one more after that eliminates Yellow and wins the game by team elimination. So I'm content to let Yellow have my Blue on (3,5) — that's a piece I can afford, and my filler for (3,4) is the Blue on (2,4) anyway.

The Red Void advances to (3,2), aiming to enter the vacant central square (3,3) on a later Red turn. Although it cannot capture, it still counts toward Team A’s center occupation and is placed where Green cannot immediately sandwich it.

**Move note.** Red is eliminated, so its surviving pieces are Void — the one that just slid to (3,2) can shuffle around and block squares, but it can never capture anything again. Yellow is Team A's only remaining teeth, and Yellow hasn't moved since taking (3,4); its turn comes next.

That pending Yellow turn is the whole issue. Yellow's one real threat is running (7,6) straight up the empty column 6 to (3,6), which would pinch my Blue on (3,5) against its own piece on (3,4). My Blue on (5,5) already walls column 5, so column 6 is the last open lane on that side — and my Blue on (6,7) is doing nothing at all. It steps left to (6,6) and slams the lane shut.

That Blue on (3,5) is worth far more than an idle rook on the back file, because it does two jobs. It's my filler for (3,4) — one step left the moment that square frees up — and it's the wall that stops Yellow from ever *re*-entering (3,4) along row 3.

Look at what the block does to Yellow's piece on (3,4): up is my Blue, down is my Blue, right is my Blue, and left is (3,3) — the only square it can legally move to. It is effectively frozen. And (3,3) is poisoned: if it steps there, my Green drops from (1,3) to (2,3) and pinches it against my Green on (4,3). So I'm deliberately keeping that Green *on* (1,3) as the executioner rather than advancing it.

Meanwhile the kill is mechanical. Captures only fire on the mover's landing square, so a Blue simply steps off (2,4) and steps back on: landing there it sees Yellow, then my own Blue on (4,4), and the piece dies. If Yellow flees into the vacated (2,4) instead, (3,4) opens and my Blue on (3,5) fills it while Green takes (3,3) — that's all four central squares and the game.

Yellow sits on one loss. Either branch takes it to two, and one more after that eliminates the color and wins by team elimination. I'll watch the (7,7)-and-up-column-7 detour now that I've vacated (6,7).
Yellow exploits the opponents’ vertical alignment: moving to (6,4) makes the Yellow on (3,4) the far flank, sandwiching and capturing both Green on (5,4) and Blue on (4,4).

**Move note.** That cost me. Yellow's move up column 4 to (6,4) ran a single line through my Green on (5,4) *and* my Blue on (4,4) to its own piece on (3,4) — a sandwich line can be any length, and both of those pieces went at once. I read the column as safe because I was checking one-square pinches. Green is now on two losses, so a third capture eliminates the color; every Green move from here has to be checked against long lines, not just adjacent squares.

Green takes (3,3), dropping down the empty column 3 from (1,3). Three reasons.

First, it's genuinely safe, which is the scarce commodity right now. Pinching it along row 3 needs matching pieces on (3,2) and (3,4) — but (3,2) holds a *Void* Red and (3,4) holds a Yellow, and mismatched colors can never combine for a sandwich. Along column 3, the far flank would have to be (2,3), and Yellow simply cannot get to rows 0-2 anywhere: my Blues wall columns 4, 5, 6 and the top of column 7. I also checked the long lines — my Green on (4,3) directly below means any downward line ends on my own color immediately.

Second, it takes a central square and denies Yellow one. I hold (3,3) and (4,3); Yellow holds (3,4); (4,4) is the open square.

Third, it shrinks Yellow's piece on (3,4) to two legal moves. Up is my Blue, right is my Blue, left is now my Green — it can only drop to (4,4) or (5,4). And (4,4) is a trap: if the *other* Yellow comes up from (6,4) to (4,4), then column 4 reads Yellow-Yellow-then-my-Blue-on-(2,4), and my Blue steps from (5,5) to (5,4) and takes **both** in one line. That's Yellow's second and third losses at once — elimination, and with Red already gone, the game.

Note I deliberately did not stack a second Green next to (4,3) in column 3, and won't: two of my pieces in a row with an open square beyond is exactly the shape that just cost me two pieces.

The Red Void moves to (4,6), taking a clear route toward the vacant center square (4,4). It cannot capture, but it still counts for Team A’s center victory and currently has a safe approach along row 4.

**Move note.** Yellow has a one-move shot that would eliminate my Green color, and everything else has to wait. Its piece on (7,1) has a completely clear column 1 all the way up to (3,1). Landing there, it looks right along row 3 and sees the Void Red on (3,2), then my Green on (3,3), then its own Yellow on (3,4) — one unbroken line of non-Yellow pieces closed by a Yellow at the far end. Both come off. Void pieces are still capturable and still count as part of the line, so Red's abandoned piece is actually acting as a bridge to my Green. That would be Green's third loss and the whole color goes Void.

This is exactly the shape that already cost me two pieces last turn: a long line, not an adjacent pinch. I'm reading the full rays now rather than just neighbouring squares.

So Blue slides from (5,5) the length of row 5 to (5,1) and corks the column. Yellow's piece can now climb no further than (6,1); rows 0-2 of column 1 are unreachable for it because my Blues wall columns 4 through 7 above, and row 3 is sealed on the left by my own Green on (3,0) and on the right by the Void Red. The threat is dead, not merely delayed.

The cost is that my right-side Blue leaves (5,5), which loosens my Blue on (6,6) a little and gives up the quick route to (5,4). I'll accept that — a whole colour is worth more than tempo.

Next I want to pull that Void Red off (3,2) permanently: my Green on (3,0) steps to (3,1) and pinches it against my Green on (3,3), which deletes the bridge and makes row 3 safe for good. I also have to answer Yellow's slower plan of reaching (6,2), where it would pinch my Green on (6,3) against the Yellow on (6,4); dropping that Green to (5,3) answers it, since a column-3 line there ends on my own pieces and the far anchor square (2,3) is unreachable for Yellow.

Yellow advances to (5,4), occupying Blue’s dangerous approach square. This prevents Blue on (5,1) from landing there to form a vertical sandwich through the center, while supporting Yellow’s piece on (3,4) along the same file.

**Move note.** Yellow dropped from (6,4) to (5,4), which quietly created two things I have to weigh. It threatens to run along row 5 to (5,6), where it would pinch my Blue on (6,6) against its own piece on (7,6) — I'll answer that with my Blue next turn. And it sets up a two-move squeeze on my Green at (6,3): Yellow needs only (5,3) and (7,3), each one move away, and since Green already carries two losses, a third capture eliminates the whole colour.

So I'm evacuating that Green rather than waiting to be forked. It slides the length of row 6 to (6,0), which is about as safe a square as exists on this board. There's no row sandwich possible against a piece on the left edge, and the column version needs Yellow on both (7,0) and (5,0) — (5,0) is unreachable for it, because row 5 is corked by my Blue on (5,1) and column 0 would be blocked by the Green itself. That piece is now effectively out of danger permanently.

I deliberately rejected the more natural-looking retreat to (5,3). Keeping row 5 **empty** is the single most important feature of my position right now. Column 4 currently reads: my Blue on (2,4), Yellow on (3,4), an empty square, Yellow on (5,4). If Yellow ever advances the lower piece to (4,4), the two Yellows stack directly under my Blue — and my Blue on (5,1) has a clear run along row 5 to (5,4), where it looks up and takes **both** in one line. That's Yellow's second and third losses at once: colour eliminated, and with Red already gone, the match. Blocking row 5 with my own Green would have thrown that away.
